reference.source: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies / WHO envenoming guidance
clinicalPearls: Latrodectism is dominated by pain and autonomic features rather than local tissue destruction; the bite site itself is often unremarkable
Pain begins locally and radiates to become regional or generalised, with muscle cramping and spasm that may involve the abdomen and mimic an acute abdomen
Diaphoresis is characteristic and may be localised or regional, sometimes with a distribution around the bitten limb
Associated features include hypertension, tachycardia, nausea, headache, tremor and restlessness
Symptoms can be prolonged and wax and wane over days; the bite is rarely life-threatening in otherwise healthy adults
Management principles centre on analgesia; antivenom may be considered for severe or refractory systemic symptoms with attention to allergic reaction risk
There is no dermonecrosis with widow bites, which helps distinguish latrodectism from recluse (loxoscelism) envenomation
reference.pathophysiology: Widow spider venom contains alpha-latrotoxin, which binds pre-synaptic nerve terminals and forms cation-permeable pores that trigger massive, calcium-independent exocytosis of neurotransmitters. Depletion and unregulated release of acetylcholine and catecholamines at neuromuscular junctions and autonomic synapses produce sustained muscle contraction, cramping and autonomic hyperactivity. The result is severe pain, diaphoresis and cardiovascular stimulation without significant local tissue necrosis, since the venom acts on nerve terminals rather than directly on tissue.
additionalDifferentials: Acute abdomen (appendicitis, perforated viscus, renal colic)
Acute coronary syndrome given chest and abdominal pain with autonomic features
Tetanus or other cause of muscle rigidity
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis based on history and characteristic syndrome
Electrocardiography if chest pain or marked hypertension is present
Creatine kinase if muscle spasm is severe or prolonged
Basic electrolytes and calcium to exclude metabolic causes of cramp
Blood pressure and pain monitoring to gauge severity and treatment response
redFlags: Severe uncontrolled hypertension with end-organ symptoms
Symptoms in pregnancy, in young children or in patients with significant comorbidity
Progressive or refractory pain and spasm despite analgesia
reference.prognosis: Latrodectism is painful and can be debilitating for days, but is very rarely fatal in healthy individuals and generally resolves fully with symptomatic care and, where indicated, antivenom.
pitfalls: Mistaking abdominal muscle rigidity for a surgical abdomen and proceeding to unnecessary laparotomy
Providing inadequate analgesia for what can be very severe, protracted pain
Expecting local necrosis and doubting the diagnosis when the bite site looks benign
Overlooking heightened risk in pregnancy, children or cardiac patients
management: Control pain with adequate analgesia, including opioids, as the mainstay of management
Relieve muscle cramping and spasm with benzodiazepines, and give antiemetics for associated nausea
Reserve widow-spider antivenom for severe or refractory systemic envenomation, weighing the risk of anaphylaxis and serum sickness
Give routine wound care and ensure tetanus immunisation is up to date
Monitor blood pressure and heart rate, obtaining an electrocardiogram where chest pain or marked hypertension occurs
Reassure that latrodectism is self-limiting and rarely fatal in healthy adults, though symptoms may wax and wane over days
Escalate for refractory pain, autonomic instability or cardiovascular compromise
